title: DLARA
official_title: To improve accountability in the disaster loan program of the Small Business Administration, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Tim Moore (R-NC) with 19 cosponsors in the Republican-led House. The bill adds reporting and oversight requirements to the SBA disaster loan program rather than new spending, the kind of accountability measure that tends to draw bipartisan support; the version that advanced pared the low-funding provision down to a notification requirement, dropping the earlier authority to limit new loan obligations.
summary: Adds accountability and reporting rules to the Small Business Administration’s disaster loan program. It requires more frequent and detailed reports to Congress, new budget disclosures, GAO reviews, and requires the SBA to notify Congress within 24 hours when disaster-loan funding runs low.
brief: Imposes new reporting, budgeting, and oversight requirements on the SBA disaster loan program and adds a low-funding notification requirement.

top_lines.headline: Disaster Loan Reporting
subs: Monthly reports must project when funding hits 10% of the latest appropriation and when it will be depleted
Reports must detail any changes to obligation and expenditure estimates
Bars official-travel funds for the Administrator until a required report is submitted

top_lines.headline: Budget Disclosures
subs: Budget must separately state SBA disaster loan and COVID-EIDL loan costs against a 10-year average
Same disclosure required for administrative costs

top_lines.headline: Low-Funding Notification
subs: SBA must notify Congress within 24 hours when funding falls below 10% of the 10-year average cost

top_lines.headline: GAO Reviews
subs: GAO reports on disbursement rates and on two 2023-2024 disaster-loan rule changes

items.main: Names the Act the “Disaster Loan Accountability and Reform Act” (the “DLARA”).
items.detail: Short-title section — establishes the bill’s citation name only; no substantive effect.
Navigational table of contents — administrative text, no substantive effect.

items.main: Defines “Administration”/“Administrator” (the SBA and its head), the four “appropriate committees of Congress,” and “SBA disaster loan” — a section 7(b) direct loan, excluding COVID-EIDL (CARES Act §1110).
items.detail: Definitions apply throughout the Act; notably the “SBA disaster loan” definition carves out COVID-era EIDL loans.

items.main: Amends the monthly disaster-loan reporting requirement so reports project the date funding will reach 10 percent of the most recent appropriation and the date funds will be depleted, and detail any changes to obligation and expenditure estimates.
items.detail: The provision amends 15 U.S.C. 636k(a). It adds a prohibition: if the Administrator does not submit a required monthly report by the deadline, no funds are authorized to be appropriated for the Administrator’s official travel until the report is submitted.

sections.label: Section 5 — Budget Request Relating to Disaster Loans

items.main: Requires the President’s budget to separately state requested amounts for SBA disaster loan costs and COVID-EIDL loan costs against their 10-year averages, with an explanation of any difference.
items.detail: Amends 31 U.S.C. 1105 to add the disclosures for both program costs and administrative costs, and defines "COVID-EIDL loan" and "SBA disaster loan" for those paragraphs.

items.main: Requires SBA to notify the Appropriations and Small Business committees of both chambers within 24 hours when the balance of funds for disaster loans falls below 10 percent of the 10-year average annual cost.
items.detail: The new paragraph (17) of 15 U.S.C. 636(b) benchmarks the trigger against the 10-year average annual cost provided in the most recent Presidential budget request under section 1105(a)(39)(A) of title 31, or, if unavailable, the 10-year average for the immediately preceding 10-year period. Section 6 also redesignates an existing statute-of-limitations paragraph as paragraph (18).

sections.label: Section 7 — GAO Report on SBA Disaster Loan Account

items.main: Directs GAO to report within 180 days on disaster-loan obligation rates and average weekly disbursements to borrowers, separated by home, business, and economic injury borrowers.
items.detail: The report covers periods anchored to October 1, 2015 and July 31, 2023. SBA must respond within 90 days with an implementation plan for any recommendations.

sections.label: Section 8 — GAO Report on Disaster Loan Changes

items.main: Directs GAO to report on the budget cost of two 2023–2024 rule changes to maximum and unsecured disaster-loan amounts.
items.detail: Covers two final rules from 2023 and 2024 on maximum and unsecured loan amounts.

items.main: Requires SBA to report within 30 days on forecasting and budget-assumption corrections, with updates every 90 days until complete.

underreported.summary: If the Administrator misses a required monthly disaster-loan report deadline, no funds are authorized to be appropriated for the Administrator’s official travel until the report is submitted.
underreported.why_unreported: Among reporting requirements, this attaches a direct personal-travel funding consequence to a missed report deadline, an enforcement mechanism distinct from the disclosure rules themselves.

gaps: The bill requires extensive reporting on disaster-loan funding but does not itself appropriate additional funds for the program.

added: New requirement to notify Congress within 24 hours when disaster-loan funding falls below 10% of the 10-year average cost (15 U.S.C. 636(b)(17))
New GAO reviews of disaster-loan disbursements and two 2023–2024 rule changes
New budget disclosures of disaster-loan and COVID-EIDL costs against 10-year averages (31 U.S.C. 1105)
modified: Expands the monthly disaster-loan report to project funding-depletion dates and estimate changes (15 U.S.C. 636k(a))

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Moore
featured_quotes.text: I will first start off with thanking my colleague on the other side of the aisle for his support on this. It is great when we can do bipartisan things, particularly on such subject matter. When Hurricane Helene struck western North Carolina and so many other States, small businesses were on the front lines of recovery. They stepped up to serve their communities and support their neighbors. They led, in a lot of ways, the response when it was needed most. When disaster hits, speed matters.

modified: Travel-prohibition penalty softened: a missed monthly report now means "no funds are authorized to be appropriated for official travel" instead of "no funds may be obligated for official travel"
Low-funding paragraph (17) cut down to the 24-hour notification requirement only — the authority to limit loan obligations, the 14-day disbursement deadline, and the 4-year sunset all dropped
SBA Inspector General review of the funding shortfall (former Sec. 9) deleted; the budget/forecasting report becomes Sec. 9
removed: Subparagraph (17)(B) authority for the Administrator to limit loan obligations to collateral-required amounts when funding is low
Subparagraph (17)(D) requirement to obligate and disburse remaining loan amounts within 14 days of new appropriations
Sec. 6(b) 4-year sunset striking paragraph (17) and Sec. 6(c) 1-year GAO report on the impact of the obligation-limit amendments
Entire SBA Inspector General review section, including review of the Oct. 4, 2024 Biden letter and Oct. 10, 2024 Administrator letter on the funding shortfall
